summary: Defines the second version of the Management Information Base (MIB-II), the set of managed objects for TCP/IP networks that network management protocols like SNMP can read. It is an Internet standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Network management software needs every device to expose the same basic information: what the device is, which interfaces it has, and counters for the main protocols it speaks. RFC 1213 defines that shared list, called MIB-II, as ten groups of named objects under the identifier mib-2. Devices answer questions about these objects using management protocols such as SNMP. The memo is an Internet Standard and says nothing about security.

questions: what is the address translation group
subtitle: The standard list of things a TCP/IP device can report about itself to a network management system.

tldr.problem: Managers of TCP/IP networks needed one agreed list of the essential facts and counters that every device exposes, so that management tools could read and set them in the same way everywhere.
tldr.mechanism: MIB-II defines managed objects with names, types and access rules, grouped under one object identifier prefix, mib-2. The groups are System, Interfaces, Address Translation, IP, ICMP, TCP, UDP, EGP, Transmission and SNMP.
tldr.outcome: It is an Internet Standard that obsoletes RFC 1158 and has been updated by RFC 2011, RFC 2012 and RFC 2013. It says nothing about security.

sections.title: Why MIB-II Exists
sections.content:
This memo defines the second version of the Management Information Base (MIB-II) for managing TCP/IP-based internets. Together with its companion memos — RFC 1155 on the structure of management information and RFC 1157 on the management protocol — it forms a simple, workable system for managing the Internet.

The introduction recounts the history. The IAB set a two-prong strategy: use the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) in the short term and examine the OSI network management framework in the long term. The first documents (RFC 1065 and RFC 1066) were designed to stay compatible with both frameworks. The strategy worked quickly in the short term, but later review found the two frameworks more different than anticipated, so the compatibility requirement was suspended. That let the operational SNMP framework respond to new needs, producing MIB-II, which supersedes MIB-I (RFC 1156) and later obsoleted RFC 1158.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators needed one agreed set of questions that any TCP/IP device could answer, so management tools work the same way everywhere. MIB-II is the second edition of that set, shaped by years of practical experience with the first edition.

sections.title: How Objects Are Defined
sections.content:
Managed objects live in a virtual information store, the MIB. Each object has a name, a syntax and an encoding. The name is an object identifier, an administratively assigned name that specifies an object type; together with an instance it identifies a specific value. The syntax is written in a restricted subset of ASN.1 as set by the SMI, purposely limited for simplicity. The SMI also specifies the ASN.1 basic encoding rules, subject to extra SNMP requirements, for how values travel on the network.

MIB-II defines two textual conventions. DisplayString is an OCTET STRING restricted to the NVT ASCII character set, conventionally declared with size 0 to 255; sysDescr and ifDescr use it. PhysAddress is an OCTET STRING for media addresses, so an Ethernet address is a string of 6 octets; ifPhysAddress, atPhysAddress and ipNetToMediaPhysAddress use it. Both conventions change neither the syntax nor the semantics of the objects that use them; they are explanatory labels only. Objects defined as plain OCTET STRING may contain arbitrary binary data.

All objects sit under the prefix mib-2 OBJECT IDENTIFIER ::= { mgmt 1 }, the same prefix MIB-I used, so existing tools keep working.
sections.plainLanguage: Every object has a unique numeric address, a data type that says what kind of answer it holds, and an access rule that says whether it can be read or also written. Two labels, DisplayString for human-readable text and PhysAddress for hardware addresses, make the definitions easier to read without changing how values work.

sections.title: Design Criteria and Extensibility
sections.content:
The list of objects was deliberately kept to essentials, following criteria carried over from MIB-I. An object had to be essential for fault or configuration management. Only weak control objects were permitted — weak meaning that tampering with them can do only limited damage — because the management protocols of the day were not sufficiently secure for more powerful control operations. Evidence of current use and utility was required. No object was allowed that could be derived from others, to avoid redundancy. Implementation-specific objects were excluded. Heavy instrumentation of critical code was to be avoided, with a general guideline of about one counter per critical section per layer. MIB-I had aimed for roughly 100 objects to ease vendors' work; MIB-II raised that limit given the wider technological base.

Keeping the list short does not limit what can be managed, because the SMI provides three extensibility mechanisms: new standard objects through new versions of the MIB, widely available but non-standard objects in the experimental subtree, and private objects in the enterprises subtree. Vendor-specific elements and experiments both fit, and proven experiments can later be elevated into the standard MIB.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors included only what operators really need, and they kept the writable objects harmless because the management protocol was not yet secure enough for stronger control. Anything extra can live in private or experimental parts of the name tree, so the standard list stays small.

sections.title: The Ten Groups of MIB-II
sections.content:
The objects are arranged into ten groups, each with its own identifier under mib-2: system (1), interfaces (2), at (3), ip (4), icmp (5), tcp (6), udp (7), egp (8), transmission (10) and snmp (11). Number 9, once allocated to CMOT, is left commented out as historical in the module. The System and Interfaces groups are mandatory for all systems; the others apply when the device implements the corresponding protocol.

The Address Translation group is deprecated because its only table, atTable, assumed a single network protocol and mappings in only one direction, from network to physical address. Multi-protocol nodes and the need for inverse mappings invalidated both assumptions, so the replacement is a translation table inside each protocol group: the IP group gained ipNetToMediaTable, which provides identical functionality, and a future CLNP MIB would define tables in both directions.

The Transmission group is a reserved prefix for definitions of particular transmission media, added when Internet-standard definitions exist; by convention a medium's subtree is named after its ifType value. The SNMP group holds statistics about SNMP itself, such as received and sent message counts. The interfaces group describes every interface through ifTable, indexed by ifIndex, with columns such as ifDescr, ifType, ifMtu, ifSpeed, ifPhysAddress, ifAdminStatus (the desired state) and ifOperStatus (the current state), plus input and output counters for octets, packets, discards and errors.
sections.plainLanguage: The objects are organized like chapters of a report: one chapter about the device itself, one about its network interfaces, and one each for the main protocols it may speak, plus chapters reserved for media-specific details and for statistics about the management protocol itself.

sections.title: Groups as the Unit of Conformance
sections.content:
Individual objects are not optional. Instead, groups are the basic unit of conformance: if the semantics of a group apply to an implementation, that implementation must implement all objects in the group. For example, an implementation must implement the EGP group if and only if it implements EGP. The System and Interfaces groups are mandatory for all systems; if an agent has no value configured for a System string object, it returns a string of length 0.

Groups serve two purposes: assigning object identifiers in a tidy tree, and telling agent implementors exactly which objects they must provide.

MIB-II also introduces the term deprecated. A deprecated object must still be supported, but will most likely be removed in the next version of the MIB. MIB-II marks only atTable as deprecated, which deprecates the entire Address Translation group; no functionality is lost, because the IP group's ipNetToMediaTable provides equivalent or superior functionality.
sections.plainLanguage: You cannot cherry-pick individual objects. If a group applies to your device, you implement all of it. A group marked deprecated must still work for now, but its replacement is already defined and will take over.

sections.title: A Few Notable Objects
sections.content:
The sysServices object is a sum over the protocol layers a node serves: for each layer L from 1 to 7 that the node performs transactions for, 2^(L-1) is added. A node that primarily routes has the value 4 (the internet layer), while a host that offers application services has 72 (end-to-end plus application layers). It ranges from 0 to 127.

The sysObjectID value is allocated under the enterprises subtree 1.3.6.1.4.1 and identifies what kind of box is being managed; the memo's example gives vendor "Flintstones, Inc." the subtree 1.3.6.1.4.1.4242 and its "Fred Router" the identifier 1.3.6.1.4.1.4242.1.1. sysUpTime counts hundredths of a second since the network management part of the system was last re-initialized. sysContact, sysName and sysLocation are read-write administrative strings.

Most objects are read-only, but a few can be set. ifAdminStatus is the desired interface state (up, down or testing) against the read-only ifOperStatus. ipForwarding is read-write, so a manager can turn routing on or off. tcpConnState is read-write only so that a management station can set it to deleteTCB(12), which deletes the connection's Transmission Control Block and terminates the connection at once; any other set attempt should get a badValue response. snmpEnableAuthenTraps can disable all authentication-failure traps regardless of other configuration, and the RFC strongly recommends storing it in non-volatile memory so the setting survives restarts.
sections.plainLanguage: Mostly you read values such as uptime, interface speed and error counters. A handful can be written: whether the device forwards packets, which interface state is desired, whether failed logins generate alerts, and one special value that kills a TCP connection immediately.

sections.title: What Changed from the Earlier MIBs
sections.content:
Compared with MIB-I (RFC 1156), the System group gained sysContact, sysName, sysLocation and sysServices. The definition of ifNumber was corrected, because it wrongly required every interface to support IP, which prevented managing devices such as MAC-layer bridges; ifTable was re-designated not-accessible, and many new ifType values were added (ppp, softwareLoopback, frame-relay and others), along with the ifSpecific column. The IP group gained ipNetToMediaTable and ipRoutingDiscards, and ipForwarding became read-write; ipRoutingTable was renamed ipRouteTable and gained ipRouteMask, ipRouteMetric5 and ipRouteInfo. The TCP group gained tcpInErrs and tcpOutRsts, the UDP group gained udpTable, and the EGP neighbor table was extended with counters and state-change objects plus a new egpAs variable. The new Transmission and SNMP groups were allocated.

Compared with RFC 1158, which this memo obsoletes, the objects are rewritten in the extended SMI conventions of RFC 1212 with semantically identical meaning. Other changes: the PhysAddress textual convention was introduced, sysLocation became read-write, several IP, EGP and SNMP object definitions were clarified, tcpConnState became read-write for connection deletion, new ifType values 29 through 32 were defined, and snmpInBadTypes and snmpOutReadOnlys were removed, with their object identifiers reserved to prevent future reuse.
sections.plainLanguage: Compared with the first edition, this one adds the objects operators asked for, fixes the interface count definition, moves address translation into the IP chapter, and retires the old translation table. Compared with the interim RFC 1158, the definitions are rewritten in clearer notation with the same meaning, plus a few access and definition fixes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section is a single sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo.

The design reflects security worries indirectly. One of the inclusion criteria is that only weak control objects are permitted, because the management protocols of the day were not sufficiently secure for powerful control operations. The writable objects that do exist were chosen so that tampering can do only limited damage, and snmpEnableAuthenTraps at least lets an operator silence repeated authentication-failure alerts.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does not discuss protections such as authentication or encryption. It only makes sure that the objects a manager can change cannot cause much harm.

items.label: established
items.desc: Connection is open and data transfer is possible.

items.label: finWait1
items.desc: Waiting for the other side's connection termination request.

items.label: finWait2
items.desc: Waiting for the other side's termination request.

items.label: closeWait
items.desc: Waiting for the local application to finish.

items.label: closing
items.desc: Both sides have sent termination requests.

items.label: timeWait
items.desc: Waiting for packets still in the network.

items.label: deleteTCB
items.desc: The only value a manager may set; deletes the TCB and ends the connection at once.
